items.title: Brookfield, CPP Complete $5.2B REIT Buyout, Pick Up U.S. Logistics Assets
items.description: Brookfield Asset Management and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board completed a $5.2B deal to take logistics operator LXP Industrial Trust off the New York Stock Exchange. Unsplash/Bernd Dittrich The two Canadian giants — BAM is the New York-based investment management arm of Toronto-based Brookfield Corp. — completed an all-cash deal to buy and delist the South Florida-based REIT and its 107-property portfolio across the Midwest and Sun Belt . Brookfield Real Estate CEO Lowell Baron said the deal for the 52M SF portfolio fit within the firm’s conviction in the long-term fundamentals of the U.S. industrial sector. The joint venture between Brookfield and CPP Investments paid $61.20 per share to delist LXP and take the company private, a 12.3% premium on LXP’s 30-day weighted average share price at the time of the offer. The deal, first announced in July , included a 40-day window in which LXP management could have sought a better buyout price. In June, management valued the then-108-property portfolio at $4.7B in a presentation to investors. The portfolio was 96.6% leased at the time with average in-place rents of $5.28 per SF. Nearly all of the portfolio was new, bulk distribution real estate. The REIT reported $49.5M in funds from operations in the second quarter , up $2.2M from the prior quarter and 5% year-over-year. It sold one property in the second quarter for $51M and acquired a 37-acre infill covered land investment in Phoenix for $103.2M. LXP also began development on two speculative projects in Columbus, Ohio. The REIT has a diversified tenant base. Its largest tenant is Amazon , which occupies 6.7% of its portfolio, and its top 10 tenants account for roughly a third of its occupancy. Its properties are spread across Arizona, Texas, Indiana, Ohio, Tennessee, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida. “With strong occupancy and exposure to key distribution markets, we believe LXP is well positioned to capture further value as logistics markets evolve, supporting attractive long-term returns for the CPP Fund,” Sophie van Oosterom , head of real estate at CPP Investments , said in a statement Monday. The U.S. industrial market has proven resilient even as developers created a glut of new construction during the pandemic. Absorption in the third quarter was at its highest rates since the start of 2023, and demand surpassed 70M for the second time in as many quarters, according to Cushman & Wakefield ’s third-quarter market report. National vacancy is at 6.8%, its lowest level since the end of 2024. items.title: Private Residential Construction Slips as Remodeling Weakens
items.description: Private Residential Construction Slips as Remodeling Weakens November 2, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Private residential construction spending decreased in September 2026 driven by a steep decline in improvement (remodeling) spending. According to the latest construction spending data from the U.S. Census Bureau, private residential construction spending came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of $848.8 billion in September, down 5.5% from the revised August estimates and lower by 8.9% from last year. The decrease in spending was primarily due to a sharp decline in improvement (remodeling) spending, which declined 13.0%. Over the year, remodeling spending was down 18.0%. Both spending on single-family and multifamily construction were unchanged from August but were down by 2.4% and 0.2% from a year ago, respectively. The decline in single-family construction spending is consistent with weak builder sentiment reflected in the NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) , amid rising interest rates, energy and material costs. The NAHB construction spending index shown in the graph below illustrates how spending on single-family construction has slowed since early 2024, reflecting the impacts of elevated interest rates and ongoing uncertainty over building material tariffs. Multifamily construction spending growth has also slowed down after the peak in June 2023, with the index largely plateauing since late 2024. In contrast, improvement spending has been on an upward trend since 2023, supported in part by the aging housing stock and sustained demand for renovation . However, the latest data is consistent with a 2026 soft patch for remodeling. Private nonresidential construction spending continued its upward trend. September’s spending rose 1.1% to a SAAR of $790.6 billion, and is 2.3% higher compared to the previous year. Data center construction, a subcategory within office cons truction , remained strong with spending increasing 8.6% month-over-month and 90.3% year-over-year, due to buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. items.title: Q3 multifamily sales jumped 139% on Vivmark deal
items.description: Q3 multifamily sales jumped 139% on Vivmark deal Although the mega-merger made 2026’s third quarter the highest on record, apartment values fell 4.6% year over year and 6.2% at an annualized rate between Q2 and Q3. Published Nov. 2, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google The Avalon at Palisades in Charlotte, North Carolina. AvalonBay Communities acquired the property before it became Vivmark. Permission granted by AvalonBay Communities Dive Brief: The third-quarter apartment sales landscape was very similar to August’s, with sluggish single-asset sales. Still, the merger of Equity Residential and AvalonBay Communities drove deal volume up 139% year over year to $114.1 billion, according to a report that data firm MSCI Real Assets shared with Multifamily Dive. The RCA CPPI for apartments declined 4.6% YOY. It fell 6.2% at an annualized rate between Q2 and Q3, as pricing deteriorated over the past four months. The annualized decline in values in each quarter has outpaced the yearly drop. In contrast, the RCA US National All-Property CPP rose 0.9% YOY. Without the creation of Vivmark, sales would have fallen 7% YOY for the quarter and been flat so far for the first nine months of the year. However, with the deal, 2026’s third quarter was the largest on record, surpassing $90.4 billion in 2021 and $78.4 billion in 2022. It was the second-largest quarter on record, falling only behind Q4 2021, which tallied $167.1 billion in trades. Dive Insight: Prices usually follow transaction growth, with investors underwriting appreciation as they bid, according to MSCI. “Here, volume is rising while prices fall, which points to a single transaction rather than broader confidence in the apartment sector,” MSCI said in the report. The usual gauge of industry health, individual sales, dropped 12% YOY to $34.3 billion in Q3, marking the second straight quarter of decline. In the six major metros, individual sales were approximately flat at $11.8 billion, while they dropped 17% YOY to $22.5 billion in non-major cities. The Vivmark deal pushed up volume across various subtypes. Portfolio sales rose 19% YOY to $10.2 billion on the strength of the Vivmark deal, while mid- and high-rise transactions jumped 248% YOY to $70.2 billion. The market was hardly thriving before the 10-year Treasury began rising six months ago. But since then volumes have declined, and cap rates have risen. In Q1 2022, cap rates sat at 4.5%, according to MSCI’s hedonic rate calculation. Now they’re 140 basis points higher. While much of that movement came in early 2024, they climbed 20 bps over the last year to 5.9% in Q3. As the 10-year Treasury moved above 5% in Q3, owners say it has become difficult to project deals they’re underwriting . “The last 60 days have been difficult, and from our end makes it difficult to pin down where we think exit caps are going,” American South Capital Partners Executive Vice President Tyler Epps told Multifamily Dive. Tyler Chesser, the co-founder and managing partner of CF Capital, said that “cap rates have moved out since the September [Federal Reserve] meeting,” and sellers are slow to accept it. “Historically it takes a few quarters for seller expectations to catch up to the market,” Chesser previously told Multifamily Dive. “Until they do, the bid-ask gap means a lot of deals stall, get retraded, or die.” Click here to sign up to receive multifamily and apartment news like this article in your inbox every weekday. items.title: The Data Center Election That Matters Isn't In Congress
items.description: Data centers have become one of the nation’s defining political issues ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. As tech giants invest hundreds of billions of dollars to build behemoth facilities and use vast amounts of power to support their artificial intelligence race, communities have pushed back. Candidates on the federal, state and local levels have responded to data center opposition by proposing stringent regulations on the industry — and by painting their opponents as data center supporters. This contentious issue could influence the control of Congress and reshape statehouses across the country. Bisnow/created with ChatGPT But for all the focus on data centers on the campaign trail, industry experts say the election’s actual impact on the development boom may be less widespread than the rhetoric would suggest. In Congress, even if a wave of anti-data center Democrats take control of both chambers, they would still struggle to pass significant legislation that could receive the signature of President Donald Trump , a vocal supporter of the industry. In many states, candidates on both sides of the aisle are supporting stricter data center rules — meaning the industry is in for a tougher road no matter who wins. But there are state-level races in the key digital infrastructure markets of Texas, Pennsylvania and Georgia where candidates have staked out different positions, and the election could determine how much data center development will be allowed to move forward. Just in those three states, Morgan Stanley estimates the planned development of 284 data centers totaling more than 33 gigawatts of capacity are at risk pending the results of these races. “I don't think at the federal level the policy is going to shift much,” MOCA Economics Chief Economist Brandon Michalski told Bisnow . “If we go to the state level, that shifts dramatically and could change the trajectory significantly.” The Battle For Capitol Hill From Ohio and Michigan to Wisconsin, Texas and Maine, data centers have emerged as a major campaign issue in high-profile House and Senate races ahead of this week’s midterms. Data centers are deeply unpopular , and congressional candidates from both parties have made proposals to rein in development or limit its impacts a core element of their campaigns as voters voice growing concerns over electricity costs, environmental impacts and the broader consequences of the AI data center boom. The trend is especially visible in political advertising . As of the beginning of October, House and Senate campaigns had spent more than $29M on ads mentioning data centers, almost always negatively, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Bisnow . Although opposition to data centers cuts across party lines, Democrats have more aggressively nationalized the issue, contrasting calls for oversight of the sector with the Trump administration’s support for accelerating AI infrastructure development. Prominent congressional Democrats have already proposed measures like a national data center moratorium and released an investigation arguing that hyperscalers aren’t paying their fair share of grid costs. Now, party leaders are signaling their intent to make more aggressive oversight of the industry a prominent part of their policy agenda following the midterms, particularly if the party gains control of one or both houses of Congress. Last week, the Senate’s top Democratic tax writer announced plans to pursue an additional excise tax on data centers while eliminating the industry’s ability to tap a range of existing tax benefits tied to depreciation, research spending, opportunity zones and REIT structures. Although Republicans have also pursued measures aimed at addressing voter concerns over data centers driving up electricity prices, GOP leaders have privately acknowledged that data centers have become a winning issue for Democrats. The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned major technology and AI firms in August that Democrats were successfully making data centers the “centerpiece” of the Senate race in Ohio and that deteriorating public sentiment toward the industry was becoming a broader risk to Republican candidates specifically. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle,” the letter warned . The data center industry has taken notice of this partisan dynamic. AI infrastructure super PAC Leading the Future and connected groups have spent significantly more supporting Republicans than Democrats, according to Forbes , while hyperscalers and AI giants like OpenAI have reportedly ramped up lobbying in anticipation of more aggressive Democratic oversight of data center development and the AI trade. Investors and analysts focused on the data center industry have similarly warned that the potential for Democratic victories in the House and Senate poses a threat to the industry’s growth and would bring greater regulatory and political risk. “There will be congressional hearings. There will be investigations,” said Brian Gardner, chief Washington policy strategist at Stifel , according to Reuters. “You never know where that stuff leads, and there can be negative headlines.” Yet despite the rhetoric and the flood of money pouring into congressional races, not everyone is convinced that even a Democratic sweep would materially change the federal regulatory environment for data centers. A report published this week by MOCA Economics examining data center construction spending projected that Democratic control of at least one chamber would be a “nothingburger for policy.” Michalski, who authored the report, said Democrats could introduce more restrictive bills, but Trump’s veto power would make measures such as a national moratorium, sweeping new grid cost requirements or additional tax burdens extremely difficult to enact. items.title: Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom
items.description: Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom Published on November 2nd, 2026 by Chen Zhao In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down. Last Week’s Highlights The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected. The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back. Upcoming Attractions It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027. Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data. Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis. items.title: Rocket posts $709M profit in Q3 despite tougher mortgage market
items.description: Rocket Companies on Thursday reported a third-quarter profit of $709 million, reversing a loss from a year ago as the Detroit-based mortgage lender expanded revenue and gained market share in purchase and refinance lending. The company reported net income of $709 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a net loss of $124 million a year earlier and a second-quarter 2026 net income of $229 million. Net total revenue nearly doubled year over year to $3.28 billion, up from $1.7 billion, while adjusted revenue rose to $2.57 billion, up from $1.87 billion. Adjusted net income fell to $419 million from $441 million in Q2 2026, and adjusted EBITDA declined to $748 million from Q2's $766 million. Mortgage production also slowed, with closed origination volume falling to $43.6 billion, down from $49.1 billion. The sequential decline in adjusted earnings came as mortgage production slowed from the second quarter, even as the company reported a slightly higher gain-on-sale margin. Rocket chief financial officer Brian Brown anticipated the slowdown during the company’s Q2 2026 earnings call, saying he expected Q3 to be “smaller than the second,” a contraction not seen in the industry since 2022. He cited rates above 6.8% and rising inflation expectations as key challenges. “Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” CEO Varun Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage , and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.” During the company's earnings call on Thursday afternoon, Krishna addressed the broader market. "Here's the truth about tough markets: They don't lie," he said. "They strip everything down to what's real. Who has the capital to keep investing? Whose model works in any cycle? Who can win their clients back? And who can move fast when it counts? This quarter did all of this." Brown said during the call that the company estimates its purchase market share approached 6.5% in Q3 2026, up from 6.2% in Q2 2026. Its refinance share reached 15.5%, compared with 14.3% from April through June. Mortgage production and servicing Rocket closed $43.6 billion in mortgage originations in the third quarter, down from $49.1 billion in Q2. Net rate-lock volume fell to $40.4 billion from $47 billion over the same period. The company’s total gain-on-sale margin edged up to 2.54% from 2.48% in Q2. Excluding correspondent lending , Rocket closed $33.5 billion in mortgage volume during the third quarter. Direct-to-consumer lending accounted for $24.6 billion, while wholesale channel Rocket Pro generated $9 billion. The correspondent channel contributed $10.1 billion in closed volume. Rocket’s mortgage servicing portfolio remained steady at about $2 trillion in unpaid principal balance across 9.1 million loans. The company sold mortgage servicing rights tied to $23 billion in unpaid principal balance during Q3, generating $379 million in proceeds. That was down from $53 billion in MSR sales and $795 million in proceeds in Q2. Rocket retained subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the servicing rights sold in the third quarter, compared with nearly 80% in Q2. Total liquidity rose to $11.4 billion at the end of Q3, up from $11.2 billion at the end of the prior quarter. The figure includes $2.7 billion in cash, $2.5 billion in undrawn credit lines and $6.2 billion in available servicing-rights and advance lines. Rocket said its combined servicing portfolio following the Mr. Cooper integration continued to support borrower recapture, with the company reaching its highest recapture levels to date. During Q3, Rocket continued to expand its use of artificial intelligence and its partnerships with real estate companies. The company said it pulled credit on nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer loan volume before borrowers spoke with a loan officer, compared with none a year earlier. Digital mortgage applications accounted for more than 40% of retail refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of nondigital leads. AI voice technology handled 65% of inbound servicing calls, resolving more than half without human assistance. Rocket also reported growth in its real estate partnerships. Redfin visitors who clicked to begin a mortgage transaction increased 50% year over year, while Redfin’s contribution to Rocket’s refinance leads more than doubled in Q3. Listings tied to its Compass partnership reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in Q2. In September, Rocket Mortgage adopted VantageScore 4.0 as its preferred credit scoring model for eligible loans. The company said its testing indicated qualifying borrowers could save an average of $1,600 in closing costs. Rocket Pro launched Orbit in October , offering eligible purchase borrowers same-day conditional approval and a 12-business-day timeline to clear-to-close. The company also extended a Compass pricing credit through the end of 2026. The partnership had generated more than $3 billion in rate locks since February. Outlook for Q4 2026 Rocket expects adjusted revenue of $2.1 billion to $2.3 billion in Q4, below the $2.5 billion to $2.7 billion range it projected for Q3 in its previous earnings report. Brown said that the company expects the market to weaken further as mortgage rates remain elevated and seasonal trends reduce activity. The company estimated purchase mortgage applications were down nearly 20% year over year, while refinance applications had fallen more than 50%. items.description: HALL Group Acquires 112,000 SF Office Building in Uptown Dallas by Taylor Williams November 2, 2026 November 2, 2026 3 DALLAS — HALL Group has acquired 2525 McKinnon Street, a 112,000-square-foot office building in Uptown Dallas. The eight-story building was constructed in 2003 at the nexus of McKinnon Street, Olive Street and Cedar Springs Road. HALL Group plans to make capital improvements to the building, including a refresh of the lobby and common areas, the addition of new spec suites and a modernization of building systems, as well as to rebrand the building as HALL Uptown. Eastdil Secured brokered the deal. The seller and sales price were not disclosed. items.title: Orange County multifamily rents continue to climb while vacancy holds
items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Orange County Multifamily Market Report hereHighlightsConditions in the Orange County multifamily market remained stable in the third quarter, with vacancy flat while rents ticked higher.The vacancy rate held steady at 4.6% for the third consecutive quarter and is 20 basis points higher year over year.Combined asking rents for all classes, vintages, and locations of multifamily in Orange County increased 0.2% during the third quarter to $2,670 per month. Year over year, asking rents are up 0.6%. Year to date, multifamily investment sales activity is outpacing 2025, while the median sale price has increased nearly 20% to $365,200 per unit. The average cap rate across all property classes is 5.0%.Orange County multifamily market overviewProperty fundamentals in the Orange County multifamily market were little changed in the third quarter, with rents remaining near previous levels and vacancy holding steady. Deliveries remain elevated compared with last year, though the pace of completions slowed. This deceleration in supply growth occurred at the same time as a decline in absorption in recent months, keeping the vacancy rate flat for the third quarter in a row. Rent trends have been mixed in recent periods. While rents declined in several submarkets, the largest decreases occurred in Santa Ana and Anaheim, which had recently been among the strongest areas for rent growth. The recent decline appears to be more of a correction following outsized gains than evidence of a broader pullback in achievable rents.Multifamily investment activity has increased this year, with the market on pace to record its highest transaction count since 2022. Median pricing is also up from last year, although trends have varied by property class. Class A properties are trading at a median price of $425,500 per unit, down 7% from last year, while Class C pricing has increased 32% to $325,900 per unit. Class C assets have accounted for roughly two-thirds of all transactions this year, while only one Class B property has changed hands. More than half of all transactions have occurred in Anaheim, while Garden Grove has accounted for approximately one-quarter of total activity. Anaheim sales have been particularly concentrated, with every transaction occurring within a five-mile radius. Cap rates are generally ranging from the mid-4% to mid-5% range depending on property class and vintage.Employment:Employment increased by 6,300 jobs year over year. Image Orange County employment growth accelerated during the third quarter, more than offsetting some earlier losses. Employment increased by 6,300 jobs year over year, a 0.4% gain.The leisure and hospitality sector remained one of Orange County’s fastest-growing industries. Employment in this sector increased 2.1% year over year, with 5,100 new positions filled.The retail trade sector also posted stronger growth than has been typical in recent years. In the past 12 months, total employment in this sector increased 0.9%, with the addition of 1,300 jobs.Forecast: The current pace of employment growth is forecast to continue throughout the remaining months of the year. In 2026, total employment in Orange County is expected to rise 0.5% with the addition of roughly 8,400 jobs.Development and permitting:The construction pipeline spiked in recent months. Image The pace of deliveries in Orange County slowed during the third quarter, though year-to-date completions have already surpassed the 2025 total. Roughly 3,200 units have been delivered in 2026, more than double the amount recorded during the same period last year.The construction pipeline spiked in recent months, with projects totaling nearly 4,000 units breaking ground in the past three months. There are now nearly 7,400 units underway, up 16% from one year ago. Multifamily permitting slowed during the third quarter, though strong activity earlier in the year has kept year-to-date totals elevated. Through the first nine months of 2026, permits were issued for more than 2,500 units, roughly 50% above the same period last year. Forecast: Completion dates have been pushed back on a few properties, reducing the number of units that are expected to be delivered this year. In 2026, approximately 4,000 units are forecast to come online, up from nearly 2,200 units delivered in 2025. Vacancy:Vacancy went unchanged for the third consecutive quarter. Image The vacancy rate in Orange County was unchanged for the third consecutive quarter, remaining at 4.6%. Year over year, vacancy is 20 basis points higher.The city of Anaheim continued to be one of the best areas for vacancy performance in Orange County. Year over year, Anaheim’s vacancy rate declined by 60 basis points to 3.7%.Vacancies have also tightened in Anaheim, where the rate has declined by 40 basis points during the past 12 months, ending the third quarter at 7.6%.Forecast: Orange County multifamily vacancy is expected to rise modestly as absorption moderates, though market fundamentals should remain resilient. The vacancy rate is forecast to reach 4.8% by year-end, up 20 basis points from one year ago.Rents:Mission Viejo has the strongest rent growth. Image Following a second-quarter rise, rent growth continued in the third quarter, with the average asking rent increasing 0.2% to $2,670 per month. Year over year, asking rents are up 0.6%. Asking rents are now $3.09 per square foot per month.Mission Viejo took the lead as the submarket with the strongest rent growth. In the past 12 months, asking rents in this area increased 3.4% to $2,774 per month. Laguna Hills trailed close behind, with rents rising 3.3% in the same period to $3,005 per month.Santa Ana was one of the only areas to record a decrease in asking rents. While this submarket posted a 1.3% dip in recent months, asking rents are still up 4.5% from the beginning of 2025.Forecast: Rent growth is expected to remain modest through the end of the year. items.title: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter
items.description: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter by ATTOM Team | Oct 29, 2026 | Foreclosures , Real Estate News - Recent Articles The national vacancy rate declined to 1.2 percent; Zombie home rate dropped slightly to 3 percent IRVINE, Calif. – October 29, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, the leading provider of property data , AI-powered analytics, and real estate intelligence solutions, today released its latest Vacant Property and Zombie Foreclosure Report showing that 1.2 percent of residential properties in the United States were vacant in the final quarter of the year. That was down from 1.3 percent in the third quarter and in the same quarter last year. The report analyzes publicly recorded real estate data collected by ATTOM — including foreclosure status, equity and owner-occupancy status — matched against monthly updated vacancy data. (See full methodology below). There were 269,195 properties in the foreclosure process in the fourth quarter, out of 105.1 million total properties analyzed. Of those properties in foreclosure, 3 percent, or 8,040 properties, were “zombies,” meaning the owners had abandoned the homes before the conclusion of the foreclosure proceedings. The fourth-quarter zombie rate was down from 3.3 percent in the prior quarter and in the same quarter last year. “The fourth-quarter data showed modest declines in both vacancy and zombie foreclosure rates nationwide,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “While trends vary from state to state, vacant and abandoned homes continue to represent a relatively small share of the nation’s housing stock.” Zombie homes on rise in majority of states The number of zombie properties rose quarter-over-quarter in 29 states. Among states with at least 50 zombie properties in the fourth quarter, the largest quarter-over-quarter increases were in Wisconsin (up 20.9 percent to 52 zombie properties), Maryland (up 19.2 percent to 180 zombie properties), Pennsylvania (up 17.2 percent to 252 zombie properties), Texas (up 15.7 percent to 192 zombie properties), and North Carolina (up 15.2 percent to 129 zombie properties). The states with sufficient data to analyze and that had the largest declines in zombie properties were Arizona (down 34.9 percent to 56 zombie properties), Florida (down 19.6 percent to 2,220 zombie properties), California (down 10.4 percent to 267 zombie properties), South Carolina (down 9.6 percent to 141 zombie properties), and Oklahoma (down 8.9 percent to 82 zombie properties). Vacancy rates below half a percent in much of Northeast The states with the highest overall home vacancy rates in the fourth quarter were Oklahoma (2.4 percent), Kansas (2.3 percent), Alabama (2.1 percent), West Virginia (2.1 percent), and Missouri (2 percent). The lowest vacancy rates were in New Hampshire (0.3 percent), Vermont (0.4 percent), New Jersey (0.4 percent), Connecticut (0.4 percent), and Idaho (0.5 percent). Ten metro areas posted no zombie properties There were 164 metropolitan statistical areas with sufficient data to include in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 100,000 residential properties and at least 50 properties in the foreclosure process. The metro areas with the highest zombie rates were Baltimore, MD (13 percent); Youngstown, OH (13 percent); Akron, OH (11.5 percent); Cedar Rapids, IA (10.7 percent); and Scranton, PA (9.4 percent). Ten of the metro areas had no zombie properties, the largest of which were Bridgeport, CT; El Paso, TX; Little Rock, AR; Fayetteville, AR; and Visalia, CA. Vacancy rates higher among investor-owned properties Institutional investors held 30.6 million homes in the fourth quarter, of which 2.7 percent, or 840,384, were vacant. The states with the highest vacancy rates for investor-owned homes were Indiana (6.5 percent), Alabama (5.8 percent), Oklahoma (5.4 percent), Kansas (5.2 percent), and Louisiana (5.1 percent). The lowest vacancy rates for investor-owned properties were in New Hampshire (0.6 percent), Vermont (0.9 percent), Utah (0.9 percent), Hawaii (1 percent), and New Jersey (1.1 percent). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Zombie rates high in several Baltimore, Indianapolis zip codes There were 2,585 zip codes with sufficient data to be included in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 1,000 residential properties and at least 25 in foreclosure in the fourth quarter. Of those, the highest zombie rates were in 21205 in Baltimore, MD (42.5 percent); 21223 in Baltimore, MD (40 percent); 46201 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); 46218 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); and 13619 in Carthage, NY (32.1 percent). Conclusion ATTOM’s fourth quarter vacancy and zombie home report found that the national vacancy rate fell slightly from the previous quarter to 1.2 percent. The national zombie home rate also dropped to 3 percent. Report Methodology ATTOM analyzed county tax assessor data for over 105.1 million residential properties for vacancy, broken down by foreclosure status and owner-occupancy status in the fourth quarter of 2026. Only metropolitan statistical areas with at least 100,000 residential properties and 50 properties in pre-foreclosure, counties with at least 50,000 residential properties and zip codes with at least 1,000 residential properties and 25 in pre-foreclosure were included in the analysis. "Zombie" Foreclosure Rate (Pct Pre-Foreclosures Vacant) The percentage of properties in the foreclosure process that are vacant because the owner has abandoned the property prior to the foreclosure being completed. items.title: MBTA Issues RFQ for Redevelopment of Lynn Commuter Parking Garage
items.description: MBTA Issues RFQ for Redevelopment of Lynn Commuter Parking Garage The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) has issued a request for qualifications from would-be redevelopers of its downtown Lynn, MA commuter parking garage. It's the first of a two-step process, to be followed by a request for proposals. The five-story garage opened in 1992 and has been partially closed since 2022 over safety concerns, ItemLive reported. Of its 948 parking spaces, approximately 350 are currently available. In December 2024, the City of Lynn and MBTA unveiled an initial concept that called for retaining part of the garage for parking while demolishing the remainder to make way for transit-oriented development. The city’s priorities for the property include a mix of residential, commercial, and transit uses, along with businesses and amenities to serve residents, workers, and visitors. MBTA's RFQ also calls for inclusionary zoning requiring 10% of housing units to be affordable to households earning 60% of the area median income. Photo courtesy of MBTA. Connect Inside The Story About Paul Bubny Paul Bubny serves as Senior Content Director for Connect Commercial Real Estate, a role to which he brings 19-plus years’ experience covering the commercial real estate industry and 35-plus years in business-to-business journalism. In this capacity, he oversees daily operations while also reporting on both local/regional markets and national trends, covering individual transactions across all property types, as well as delving into broader subject matter. He produces 11-15 daily news stories per day and works with the Connect team and clients to develop longer-form content, ranging from Q&As to thought-leadership pieces. Prior to joining Connect, Paul was Managing Editor for both Real Estate Forum and GlobeSt.com at American Lawyer Media, where he oversaw operations at both publications while also producing daily news and feature-length articles. His tenure in B2B publishing stretches back into the print era, and he has served as Editor in Chief on four national trade publications. Since 1999, Paul has volunteered as the newsletter editor of passenger rail advocacy groups (one national, one local). items.title: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter
items.description: Student Housing Construction Rises in the Third Quarter October 30, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Private fixed investment in student dormitories rose 2.6% in the third quarter of 2026, reaching a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of $3.8 billion. This gain marked a second consecutive quarterly increase, despite continued pressures from elevated interest rates. On a year-over-year basis, investments in dorms increased 1.1%. Private fixed investment in student housing experienced a surge after the Great Recession, as college enrollment increased from 17.2 million in 2006 to 20.4 million in 2011. However, during the pandemic, private fixed investment in student housing declined drastically from $4.4 billion (SAAR) in the last quarter of 2019 to $3.1 billion in the second quarter of 2021. According to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center , college enrollment fell by 3.6% in the fall of 2020 and by 3.1% in the fall of 2021. The latest preliminary data indicated that college enrollment held steady in fall 2026 compared with the previous year. Since the pandemic, private fixed investment in dorms has rebounded alongside a gradual recovery in college enrollments. Effective in-person learning requires college students to return to campuses, boosting the student housing sector. Still, demographic trends are reshaping the outlook for student housing. The U.S. faces slower growth in the college-age population as birth rates declined following the Great Recession. Furthermore, changing perceptions towards the value of a college degree as a guaranteed pathway to job security are all contributing to an “enrollment cliff”. items.title: Open Real Estate gets a boost from independents — and an opening from MLSs
items.description: A week after Open Real Estate , a broker-led initiative to build a shared infrastructure for residential listing data, launched , the initiative announced that it has secured 826 letters of support from real estate brokerage leaders across the country. Independent firms account for the majority of that backing, with 493 letters, or 59%, coming from independent brokerages, according to an announcement on Monday. Support spans single-office independents to some of the largest independent firms , including Atlanta Communities , Iron Valley Real Estate , LoKation Real Estate and Realty of America , all RealTrends Verified brokerages. The effort is designed as a national, shared data layer that connects brokerages, agents, multiple listing services and real estate portals. Founding organizations include AGNT Inc . (parent to eXp Realty and NextHome ), HomeServices of A m erica , Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group , all RealTrends Verified brokerages. “We have already received significant interest from across the real estate industry since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers,” the founding members of Open Real Estate said in a joint statement. MLS leaders signal willingness to collaborate Open Real Estate’s backers say the project is meant to complement, not replace, existing MLS organizations by expanding access to listing information for brokerages, agents and consumers. Several prominent MLS executives publicly welcomed collaboration with the initiative. “We welcome the initiative of Open Real Estate and look forward to actively participating and partnering with industry leaders to build on the capabilities already in place at Bright and advance a more connected, efficient, broker-driven marketplace,” Brian Donnellan, the president and CEO of Bright MLS and a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. Art Carter, CEO of California Regional MLS (CRMLS), added that the effort aligns with CRMLS’s long-running work to give brokers more flexibility in how they input and manage listing data. “Strategically, California Regional MLS and Open Real Estate are in alignment with the concept of allowing brokers to bring listing data in from outside the CRMLS MLS Input Platform. It has been a long-term project of CRMLS to allow our brokers to have that ability,” Carter, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “We look forward to working with Open Real Estate to see how that possibility comes to fruition within their platform.” North Texas Real Estate Information Systems (NTREIS) CEO Chris Carrillo framed Open Real Estate as part of a broader conversation about transparency and equal access to listings. “NTREIS remains dedicated to fostering a transparent, cooperative and neutral marketplace that serves all broker participants equally by delivering consistent listing access and empowering exceptional consumer service. In alignment with this mission, we welcome constructive dialogue with Open Real Estate,” Carrillo said. And NorthstarMLS President and CEO Tim Dain emphasized that broker-driven projects can coexist with MLSs. “Broker-led innovation shouldn’t be viewed as a threat to the MLS. It’s an opportunity to strengthen the cooperation that has served our industry for decades,” Dain, also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “I hope this initiative brings even more brokers and MLSs to the table.” The push for a shared listing data infrastructure comes as the industry adapts to rapid changes in how listings are distributed and displayed, ongoing antitrust scrutiny and shifting brokerage business models. Brokerages are looking for more direct control over how their listing data flows to MLSs, portals, internal systems and third-party tools. Open Real Estate’s founders position the initiative as a way to streamline listing distribution, expand access to housing inventory and support a more open, competitive housing marketplace, particularly as consumer expectations for transparent, real-time listing information continue to rise. Related More: Clear Cooperation MLS

items.title: Two Charts: Resilience of U.S. Single-Family Housing
items.description: Two Charts: Resilience of U.S. Single-Family Housing November 2, 2026 --> Two Charts is a research series from Pretium that provides focused, data-driven analysis of the trends shaping real estate and the broader economy. Each edition highlights a key market insight through two concise, high-impact visuals. In this edition, we examine why U.S. single-family home prices have remained resilient even as other real estate sectors have experienced significant corrections. Structural housing demand, years of underbuilding, and the interest rate lock-in effect have constrained supply and supported home values through changing market conditions. View the full analysis here .

items.title: Pennymac sees more layoffs as originations plummet in 3Q
items.description: Pennymac sees more layoffs as originations plummet in 3Q By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published October 29, 2026, 7:27 p.m. EDT | Updated October 29, 2026, 8:21 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Pennymac posted its lowest mortgage origination and acquisition volume since the first quarter of 2024. Supporting Data: While the company posted a $7 million loss in production segment pretax income, its servicing pretax income rose to $99 million. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. PennyMac Financial Services is making deeper cost cuts after its originations fell 30% this summer. The lender and servicer will slash $160 million in annualized operating expenses in the coming months as it anticipates higher-for-longer rates, it said Thursday. That expands on cuts that began this summer in response to some of the worst mortgage market conditions this decade. Processing Content While the company remained well in the black for the third quarter, its combined origination segment volume of $24.4 billion was its lowest mark since the first quarter of 2024. Chairman and CEO David Spector, in an earnings call Thursday evening, described the current landscape as "one of the most constrained origination environments our industry has seen since 2023." Pennymac didn't provide additional details about staff reductions . For the third quarter, Pennymac posted a $29 million profit, surpassing the $22 million net income in the second quarter. That was still a fraction of the $181.5 million profit Pennymac posted at the same time last year. Although elevated rates and heightened competition battered origination performance, the company highlighted stronger income in servicing, and green shoots in artificial intelligence advancements. Inside the numbers The company posted a $7 million loss in production segment pretax income, after marks of $38 million and $122.9 million in the prior quarter and year-ago periods, respectively. Servicing pretax income meanwhile rose to $99 million, soaring from $22 million in the second quarter but falling from $157 million a year ago. Pennymac also agreed to sell $29 billion in unpaid principal balance of low-rate conventional mortgage servicing rights, it said. It plans to redeploy the $490 million in proceeds to reduce higher-cost debt, and repurchase common shares. The servicing book ended the quarter slightly up around $737 billion. Revenues fell to end the period at $469 million, declines of 6% quarterly and 26% annually. Executive outlook Company leaders expanded on origination trends, with Pennymac posting greater consumer direct margins with more closed-end second lien volume. Spector also suggested competitive pressures from the government-sponsored enterprises' cash window for smaller brokerages, and the industry leaders' aggressive pricing. "We're picking and choosing our spots, and maintaining market share, and not really getting too caught up in market share at levels that are just not sustainable or that one can rationalize," said Spector. Pennymac also touted its AI advancements, noting that its tech spending is coming down. The lender has 22 proprietary AI agents live in production and is developing 17 more, while its proprietary AI voice agent supported over 1,600 rate locks in the third quarter. "This will allow us to maintain lean operation in today's constrained environment, while ensuring substantial operating leverage when origination volumes normalize," Spector said of the company's AI prowess. What's ahead The firm also announced some executive moves, as President and Chief Mortgage Banking Officer Doug Jones will retire next June. Chief Strategy Officer Kevin Ryan will be elevated to chief financial officer in January, while current CFO Daniel Perotti will remain in that role through the end of the year. Pennymac's Cenlar deal, which will bring its servicing book past $1 trillion , is now expected to close early next year, as executives said they're waiting on one remaining state approval.
